Everything decided so far, and where the build starts

Research, a product spec, a clickable prototype, ten architecture decisions and a build plan for OpenAct: free for everyone, works offline, keeps scripts on their own device, and gets the pages right in fifteen formats. Version 2 adds a review that checks a script before it goes out; version 3 adds spelling and grammar.

Research

Why OpenAct should exist

Paid screenwriting tools cost up to $250. Free tiers cap scripts, watermark exports or want a subscription, and the fully free apps each run on a single platform. Stage writers have it worse: no tool found treats pantomime structure as a feature, and musical writers format songs by hand.

ToolFree, no caps or watermarkIn a browserOffline, no accountUK and US stageSongs and lyricsPanto structure

Fade InNoNoYes??No
WriterDuetNoYesNoPartly?No
Arc StudioNoYesNo??No

ScrivenerNoNoYesYesNoNo
OpenAct (target)YesYesYesYesYesYes

"?" means no source was found. Prices and limits were checked on 3 November 2026 and change often.

For UK stage writers and for screenwriters who want professional pages without paying, OpenAct is a free, local-first app that gets the format right for stage and screen, exports clean A4 or US Letter PDF and Word files, and keeps every script on the writer's device.

Spec

What the first version does

Writing

  • Enter and Tab move through script elements, with suggestions for names and places
  • Find and replace, and renaming a character everywhere
  • Fifteen formats on A4 or US Letter, switchable at any time
  • Real pages with correct breaks, (MORE) and (CONT'D)

Structure

  • Outline of acts and scenes with drag to reorder
  • Title page and cast list
  • Numbered songs with singers and dramatic function
  • Line counts and a who's-in-which-scene chart
  • Notes that never print

Files

  • Open Fountain, Final Draft and pasted text, with a check before anything lands
  • Save as PDF, Word, Fountain or Final Draft, never watermarked
  • Autosave, snapshots, and prompts to keep a backup
  • Works offline once loaded

Everyone

  • Readable and editable on a phone
  • Keyboard-first, WCAG 2.2 AA
  • Smooth in a 150-page script
  • A first formatted page in under two minutes

After the MVP: version 2 (the review) and version 3 (spelling and grammar), then index cards, story trackers, revision mode, rehearsal scripts and co-writing.

Formats

Fifteen formats, each with its own furniture

GroupFormatsWhat OpenAct numbers and lays out for you
FilmScreenplay(MORE) and (CONT'D) at page breaks; A4 or US Letter
TelevisionOne-hour drama, single-camera comedy, multi-camera sitcom, UK studio sitcom, vertical micro-dramaActs on new pages, closed by END OF ACT; lettered or numbered scenes with the cast listed under each; double-spaced multi-camera dialogue; numbered episodes
TheatreUK and US stage plays, UK and US musicals, pantomimeSpeaker beside or above the speech; numbered songs with singers and function; front-cloth and full-stage scenes
AudioUK radio drama, audio drama and podcastCue numbers that restart on each page; sound cues; double-spaced speeches
ComicsComic or graphic novelPAGE ONE (FOUR PANELS), panel numbers, and lettering numbered for the letterer
DocumentsTreatment or outlineHeadings and prose

Each format starts from an original template. Show- and network-branded templates are left out because the names belong to others; two-column AV scripts come later.

Design

The prototype

The margin speaks

The current element's name sits in the left margin in pencil, as a stage manager annotates a prompt copy. It teaches the element names without a tutorial.

A real highlighter

Pick a character and their lines are highlighted, the way actors mark their scripts.

Bring your own format

Import a Final Draft or Word template, check a sample page, and save it as a format. A built-in finder lists common formats and links to each organisation's own page; searching it sends nothing anywhere.

Video game scripts

Nodes, player choices, conditions, barks and quest beats, with a branch map that checks every jump and recording line IDs you can lock. Exports a recording sheet, Ink and Yarn Spinner files.

Revision-paper colours

Full stage Front cloth Songs borrow the pale colours of revised script pages, always with a label.

Automated accessibility checks (axe) report no violations in light, dark and phone views. The script is a single tab stop; Esc then Tab leaves it. Still open: a pass with VoiceOver and NVDA.

Version 2

Ready to submit?

The layout engine guarantees the formatting. What drifts while a script is redrafted is another matter: length, a stale title page, your name left in for a blind read, TK placeholders and notes, a character renamed in some cues but not others, act breaks that no longer match, songs without lyrics. The review checks those against where the script is going, and shows its sources.

Ten targets

  • An agent, manager or producer
  • Academy Nicholl Fellowships, Austin Film Festival, BBC Writersroom, Bruntwood Prize
  • UK new-writing theatre, a US theatre's literary office, new musical programmes
  • A comics publisher, BBC radio drama

Four answers

  • Fix breaks a rule, such as your name in a blind entry
  • Consider a convention you can set aside for this script
  • Passed nothing to do
  • Note: information only, such as a running-time estimate

Shows its working

  • Every check names its sources, what kind they are (official rules, a listing, an industry guide, writer advice) and their date
  • Each target says when its rules were researched and links to the current ones
  • A "Before you send" list covers what OpenAct can't check

Changes nothing by itself

  • Fix buttons only for safe changes: remove a draft date, add someone to the cast list, make exports anonymous
  • An anonymous export shows the title only and leaves the PDF's author field empty

The sources, gathered on 8 November 2026, are listed in docs/research/submission-checks.md. Every rule was then confirmed against the official sites or consistent listings; that pass found that 2026–27 Nicholl entries now come only through official partners and that Bruntwood excludes pantomime.

Tested

Works offline, downloaded or installed

The same test ran four ways: open a sample, type, autosave, open the review, reload. Once the fonts were bundled with the app, all four behaved the same.

Opened asReady inEdit kept after reloadOther sites called
Hosted, online0.8 sYesGoogle Fonts
Installed app, online0.6 sYesNone
Installed app, offline0.04 s (cache)Yes, even offline editsNone
Downloaded file, offline0.8 sYesNone (all blocked)

Chromium only; Safari and Firefox are tested in build slice 12. The installable app passed Chrome's install check with no errors. Details: docs/research/offline-check.md. The downloadable file is prototype/offline/dist/openact-offline.html in the kit.

Legal

Can you give it away?

Very likely, yes. Copyright protects code, artwork and text, not features, file formats or the layouts writers are expected to follow, as courts have held in the UK, EU and US (SAS v World Programming, Navitaire v easyJet, Lotus v Borland). That holds whether it is free or sold, so the risk lies in what you copy and what you call things.

RiskLevel nowWhat to do
Copying another app's code, screens, icons, help text or templatesLowBuild everything yourself; now a rule in CLAUDE.md
Naming Final DraftMediumOnly to describe compatibility, in plain text, with a not-affiliated line
Your own app nameMediumSearch the registers and consider filing a UK mark before launch
Open-source notices and the GPL source offerMediumA licences screen and a link to the source
Fonts loaded from GoogleMediumSelf-host them; done in the offline editions
Lost work and marketing claimsMediumBackups, honest wording, a no-warranty notice
Sharing, sync, co-writing and AI featuresHigh, once builtA legal review before building them

Not legal advice. Prepared with the legal plugin's risk-assessment and compliance-check frameworks (docs/legal/legal-review.md, 38 sources). Have a UK IP and technology solicitor review the name, the marketing copy and Final Draft compatibility before launch.

One slice per Claude Code session, each tested before the next starts.

Milestone 1: write a panto in OpenAct

    Built: lint, type-check, tests and build pass. Waiting for a GitHub repository to run them automatically

  2. Model and OpenAct Fountain

    Every Fountain rule tested; samples round-trip exactly

  3. Layout engine

    Every page-break rule has a golden test; 150 pages in under 200 ms

    Breaks match the engine; typing stays under 50 ms

    20 crash tests, at most two seconds lost

  7. PDF export

    Matches the page view within half a point

    Every acceptance test for those requirements passes

Milestone 2: public release (version 1)
  1. Format library

    TV, audio, comics and treatments, each rule with a golden test

  2. Counts, chart and paste

    Pasted scripts typed at least 95% right

  3. Word and Final Draft

    Opens cleanly in Word, LibreOffice and Google Docs

  4. Offline, install and phone

    The four-way offline test passes in three browsers

  5. First run, accessibility, release

    4 of 5 new writers format a page in under two minutes; launch legal actions done

Milestone 3: version 2, ready to submit
  1. Submission review

    Every check tested at every status; an anonymous PDF holds no name, in text or metadata

Milestone 4: version 3, spelling and grammar
  1. Language engine

    Planted errors found; no character name ever flagged

  2. Marks and suggestions

    Every action works by keyboard and screen reader

  3. Grammar download

    Works offline once downloaded; off in dialogue by default

    Issues listed in the review; dialect and dictionary saved with the script

Your part

What only you can do

Ticks are saved in this browser only.

The name: OpenAct

The first choice, ActOne, turned out to be taken, so the app is now OpenAct, written as one word. It has not been searched yet: search the UK, EU and US trade mark registers (classes 9 and 42), GitHub and the app stores before launch, and expect near-matches, since "Open" names are common in open-source software. Always pair it with "the free script editor".

NameWhy it fitsClash risk

Twelve names are ranked in docs/research/names.md, and twenty more were ruled out because apps or brands already use them (Ghost Light, Callboard, Off Book, Draftline and others). "OpenAct" itself is crowded with teleprompter apps for actors and creators.

Prompt 1: the design kickoff (already run) 
I want to design a free app for writing scripts: screenplays, stage plays, musicals and pantomimes. I write panto and stage musicals myself and want screenplays too. You're the product designer and architect. This session produces an approved design in docs/; building comes later, one slice per session.

## Why it should exist (my hunch: test it in research)
Industry tools are expensive, and free tiers tend to cap scripts, watermark exports or keep your work in their cloud. Stage writers have it worse: screenwriting apps treat stage formats as an afterthought, so panto and musical writers end up fighting Word templates.

## Principles (trace every design decision to one)
1. Free for writers, always: unlimited scripts, every export, no watermark, no account.
2. Local-first: works offline; scripts stay on the writer's device until they choose to export, share or sync.
3. Open formats: Fountain is first-class; FDX and DOCX in and out; PDF out. Writers can always leave with their work.
4. Format is the product: pages look right first time, because readers judge format before story.
5. The page is the interface: keyboard-first, smart Tab/Enter flow between elements, chrome out of the way.
6. £0 running cost, a domain name aside: static hosting. Anything with an ongoing cost (sync, live co-writing, AI) is optional and sits behind its own module boundary.
7. Accessible (WCAG 2.2 AA), quick on an old laptop, usable on a phone.

## Formats
Format profiles: Screenplay (film and TV); Stage play (UK and US layouts); Musical (stage play plus song spots and lyrics); Pantomime (stage play plus full-stage/front-cloth scenes, routines, songsheet and walkdown). US Letter and A4. The rules live in the script-formats skill (.claude/skills/script-formats/); read it before any format work.

## MVP (this list is the scope; park every other idea in docs/later.md)
- Editor: smart elements, Tab/Enter flow, auto-caps, autocomplete (characters, locations, times of day, extensions, transitions), dual dialogue.
- Page view with accurate pagination, page count, and a runtime estimate for screenplays.
- Outline of acts and scenes: jump to any scene, drag to reorder.
- Title page, cast list, and song list (number, title, singers, dramatic function).
- Character-by-scene chart and line counts, for casting and rehearsals.
- Notes that never print.
- Import Fountain, FDX, DOCX and pasted text, with a review step to fix detected elements. Export PDF, DOCX, Fountain and FDX.
- Autosave, snapshots and crash recovery; open and save real files where the browser allows.
- Installable PWA: offline, light and dark, focus mode.

Later (design so these fit): index cards; setup/payoff, running-gag and topical-joke trackers (topical jokes get a check-before date); revision mode; rehearsal scripts with line numbers and cues; live co-writing; audio drama; PDF import; an opt-in AI collaborator that gives feedback on structure and continuity while the writer does the writing, using the writer's own API key.

## How we work
In phases. Each phase writes its outputs to docs/, ends with a five-line summary and open questions, then waits for my go-ahead. docs/decisions.md is the running log: date, decision, reason, source.

### Phase 0: Decisions
- Interview me with anthropic-skills:grill-me until each of these has an answer or an agreed default: who it's for first; which formats ship first; browser only, or a desktop wrapper too; default paper size; licence; how much co-writing matters; the three scripts I'll dogfood with.
- Write a short CLAUDE.md: the principles, plus pointers to docs/ and the script-formats skill.

Done when: every decision is in decisions.md.

### Phase 1: Research (docs/research/)
- anthropic-skills:deep-research and product-management:competitive-brief on Final Draft, Fade In, WriterDuet/WriterSolo, Arc Studio, Celtx, Highland, Trelby, Beat, Story Architect (formerly KIT Scenarist), Afterwriting and Scrivener, plus every stage, musical or panto tool you find (shared Word templates count). For each: price, free-tier limits, platforms, file formats, stage and musical support, standout features, top three complaints. Every price and limit gets a dated source.
- Check the script-formats skill against the sources it lists; fill gaps with anthropic-skills:skill-creator.
- design:user-research: a 30-minute interview guide and a short survey for screenwriters and for amateur-theatre writers and directors; proto-personas and jobs-to-be-done, each claim marked evidence or assumption.

Done when: competitors.md has a row per tool with every cell filled or marked unknown; gaps.md ranks the ten biggest unmet needs with evidence; positioning.md holds a one-paragraph positioning statement; every script-formats rule the MVP relies on has a logged source or an "unverified" flag.

### Phase 2: Spec (docs/prd.md)
- product-management:product-brainstorming to challenge the positioning and the MVP cut with me, then product-management:write-spec: problem, personas, jobs, MVP with acceptance criteria per feature, the later list, risks, and success measures that need no tracking (dogfood tasks done, export fidelity, issues filed).

Done when: every MVP feature has testable acceptance criteria and traces to a gap or a dogfood task.

### Phase 3: UX and visual design (docs/design/)
- Map the core flows: first run to a correctly formatted page in under two minutes; import an existing script; write a scene keyboard-only; add a song; reorder scenes; export a PDF and a Word file for a director; recover after a crash; edit on a phone, which has no Tab key (design an element switcher bar).
- anthropic-skills:frontend-design for the visual direction: calm, writerly, with the page as the hero. anthropic-skills:web-artifacts-builder for a clickable prototype of the editor, outline, song list and export.
- design:design-system for tokens and components, light and dark. design:ux-copy for empty states, element hints ("Tab → Character"), errors and export dialogs.
- design:design-critique, then design:accessibility-review, on the prototype.

Done when: the prototype covers every core flow, and every review finding is fixed or logged with a reason.

### Phase 4: Architecture (docs/adr/)
- engineering:architecture, one ADR per decision: editor framework (ProseMirror/TipTap, CodeMirror 6 or Lexical, judged on structured elements, IME and mobile input, Yjs bindings and accessibility); document model and source of truth (Fountain text or a JSON model); storage (IndexedDB or OPFS, File System Access API); PDF and DOCX libraries; desktop wrapper; licence; the path to sync and co-writing.
- engineering:system-design for the module map and data model, anchored on a single layout engine: pure TypeScript, (script, format profile, paper) → pages. The page view and the PDF export both render its output, so screen and paper always match.
- Use Context7 for current library docs.
- Starting point for the ADRs to confirm or overturn: TypeScript, Vite, React, ProseMirror, Dexie, pdf-lib, docx, Vitest, Playwright, static hosting on Cloudflare or GitHub Pages.

Done when: every MVP feature maps to a module, and every dependency has a one-line justification and a licence.

### Phase 5: Test strategy and build plan (docs/testing.md, docs/plan.md)
- engineering:testing-strategy, covering: parser tests from the Fountain spec; golden pagination tests (fixtures with expected page breaks, plus reference PDFs I supply, with their breaks extracted using anthropic-skills:pdf); round trips (Fountain ↔ model ↔ FDX); Playwright tests for the Tab/Enter flow; axe accessibility checks; a performance budget, e.g. keystroke to screen under 50 ms in a 150-page script.
- anthropic-skills:creative-writing-partner: please draft three short original sample scripts for onboarding: a screenplay scene, a panto front-cloth scene, and a musical scene with a song spot.
- plan.md: vertical slices in build order, each with a done-when line. Suggested order: script model and Fountain parser; layout engine with golden tests; editor and element flow; page view; PDF export; storage and autosave; outline; title page and cast list; stage, musical and panto profiles; song list and character chart; DOCX and FDX; PWA; polish.

Done when: every slice has a done-when line someone else could check.
